examples.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} - 3y = 12\sinh 3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\qquad$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14044108/assets/ae29bceba4d6a1f250f244b26583abeb4b8c2fbe33d380dfa4332b051bb21078.png).

$\qquad$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x) =$  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14044108/assets/c6725d6cd732c1ca7f21ab9a8dac245bc396c04a623cfb8e2eda31751ddaa89e.png).

$\qquad$ Therefore, the particular solution is $y_p(x) =$  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14044108/assets/1d1c8a545fb741413f7cdd2f6f3fa6190fbdda74290e206cc4a7f8061f97ff53.png).
examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution $y_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
y_c' - 3y_c = 0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c  = Ae^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable $y_p,$ we set $A = u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
y_p(x) = u(x)e^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of $y_p$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate $u'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =12\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =12\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =12\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =12\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =12{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\sinh 3x = \dfrac{e^{3x} - e^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =12{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\  & =12{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =6-6{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6-6{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 6-6{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =6x+{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $y_p = u(x)e^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =6x{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y={e}^{2x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{6x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$
